summary: The recent feature additions (on‑device OCR, calendar date picker, and category management) did not introduce any new critical or high‑severity flaws, but a number of medium‑severity code issues remain unaddressed. Deployment‑level dependency vulnerabilities (braces, node‑forge, sprintf‑js) are still open and must be mitigated at the hosting level before production. The OCR implementation appears to have lost the earlier image‑size validation, re‑exposing a denial‑of‑service vector. Existing high‑severity issues (data‑reset photo leak) stay fixed, and the low‑severity XSS risk in custom categories is still mitigated.

findings.issue: No size or dimension validation is performed before passing a receipt image to expo‑text‑extractor. An attacker could supply an extremely large or malformed image, causing high memory consumption and potentially crashing the app (local denial‑of‑service).
findings.fix: Add a guard that checks the image file size and dimensions (e.g., reject files >5 MiB or >3000 px in either dimension) before calling recognizeReceiptText. Offer a friendly error message and optionally downscale the image before OCR.

findings.issue: No validation of the receipt image size or dimensions before invoking expo‑text‑extractor. Maliciously large or malformed images can consume excessive memory and crash the app on the device.
findings.fix: Add pre‑validation (e.g., using expo‑file‑system to read the file size or inspect image dimensions) and reject images exceeding a safe threshold (e.g., >5 MiB or >3000 px) before calling extractTextFromImage.

findings.issue: restoreBackup decrypts the entire encrypted blob before any size checks. Supplying an extremely large backup (e.g., >10 MiB) can exhaust device memory and cause the app to crash.
findings.fix: Enforce a size limit on the encrypted backup data (reject >10 MiB) *before* decryption and also cap the number of receipts/mileage entries in validateBackupStructure (e.g., ≤10 000 receipts, ≤5 000 mileage entries). Abort early if limits are exceeded.

findings.issue: Failed restore attempts do not have any rate‑limiting or delay, allowing an attacker to brute‑force the backup passphrase offline with rapid retries.
findings.fix: Implement exponential back‑off (1 s, 2 s, 4 s, …) after each failed attempt and lock the restore UI after a configurable number of consecutive failures (e.g., 5). Store the failure count in memory and reset it on app restart.

findings.issue: CSV generation only prefixes a single quote for cells that start with =, +, -, or @. It does not fully escape commas, quotes, newlines or other special characters, leaving the exported CSV vulnerable to formula injection in spreadsheet programs.
findings.fix: Replace the hand‑rolled CSV builder with a standards‑compliant library such as csv‑stringify, or implement full RFC 4180 escaping for every field (double‑quote fields containing commas, quotes, newlines, and prefix with a single quote only when needed).

findings.issue: createBackup and restoreBackup accept any passphrase length. Although the UI enforces a 12‑character minimum, programmatic callers could supply a short passphrase, producing weakly protected backups.
findings.fix: Add an explicit length check at the start of both createBackup and restoreBackup (e.g., if passphrase.length < 12 throw an error). This guarantees the policy is enforced regardless of the caller.

findings.issue: restoreBackup writes receipt photos using the photoUri stored in the backup payload via FileSystem.writeAsync. An attacker‑controlled URI can lead to path traversal or overwriting files outside the app sandbox.
findings.fix: Ignore photoUri from the backup. When restoring, write each receipt photo to a trusted internal directory (e.g., FileSystem.documentDirectory) with a filename derived from the receipt ID, and validate that the resolved path remains within that directory before writing.

deployment_actions.issue: `braces` 3.0.3 is vulnerable to CVE‑2026‑93687 (Denial‑of‑Service via stack overflow from deeply nested patterns). No patched release exists yet.
deployment_actions.fix: No fixed release exists yet: monitor the advisory and upgrade as soon as one ships; confirm whether the package is only a build-time dependency. Monitor the package for a patched release (>= 3.0.4) and upgrade as soon as it is available. If the library is only a build‑time dependency, consider removing it from the production bundle.

deployment_actions.issue: `node‑forge` 1.4.0 contains CVE‑2026‑85393 (signature forgery vulnerability in RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 verification).
deployment_actions.fix: No fixed release exists yet: monitor the advisory and upgrade as soon as one ships; confirm whether the package is only a build-time dependency. Upgrade to a version that fixes the issue (>= 1.5.0) when released, or replace the usage of `node‑forge` with a modern, audited library such as the `@noble/*` crypto suite. Remove the dependency from `package.json` if it is not required at runtime.

deployment_actions.issue: `sprintf‑js` 1.0.3 is vulnerable to CVE‑2026‑97058 (Denial‑of‑Service via unbounded precision specifiers).
deployment_actions.fix: No fixed release exists yet: monitor the advisory and upgrade as soon as one ships; confirm whether the package is only a build-time dependency. Upgrade to a patched version (if available) or replace the library with native template literals or a safe formatting utility such as `format` from the standard library. Remove the dependency if it is only transitive.
